name: FHA loans
reg: Federal Housing Administration · HUD-insured loans · National Housing Act

items.text: An FHA loan is insured by HUD, so a borrower can qualify with a smaller down payment and a lower credit score than a conventional loan requires — as little as 3.5% down, a 96.5% LTV. In exchange, it carries mortgage insurance in two parts — an up-front premium of 1.75% of the base loan, usually financed into the loan, and an annual premium collected monthly with the payment.

How much a borrower puts down depends on their credit score. FHA sorts borrowers into three tiers. First, a score of five hundred eighty or higher earns the minimum three and a half percent down, a ninety-six point five percent LTV. Second, a score of five hundred to five seventy-nine still qualifies, but must put ten percent down, a ninety percent LTV. Third, below five hundred, there is no FHA financing at all. A weaker credit profile doesn't close the door; it raises the down payment, since FHA's insurance covers only so much of the lender's risk.

The annual MIP doesn't always run for the full term — how long it lasts turns on the down payment. Put at least 10% down and it falls off after 11 years; put less than that, and the borrower pays it for the life of the loan. Since most FHA borrowers put the minimum 3.5% down, the insurance usually runs for the life of the loan — a standing cost that makes refinancing out of FHA a common goal once the borrower has built enough equity.
